report:
Your skepticism is understandable, but the claim is broadly **supported** when stated precisely: in HBsAg-positive pregnant people with **high HBV DNA** (commonly >200,000 IU/mL, or HBeAg-positive where DNA testing is unavailable), **tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in late pregnancy lowers—but does not eliminate—mother-to-child transmission**, alongside timely birth-dose vaccine plus HBIG.

A randomized trial reported reduced transmission with third-trimester tenofovir versus placebo (https://nyulangone.org/news/antiviral-treatment-during-pregnancy-reduces-mother-child-transmission-hepatitis-b). A 2020 systematic review/meta-analysis informing WHO concluded peripartum antiviral prophylaxis, especially TDF, is highly effective at reducing HBV MTCT (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(20)30586-7/abstract). WHO therefore recommends peripartum TDF prophylaxis for high-risk HBsAg-positive pregnant women (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/978-92-4-000270-8), and AASLD guidance similarly supports antiviral therapy around the third trimester when maternal HBV DNA exceeds about 200,000 IU/mL (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6385899/).

Key caveats: benefit is clearest at high viral load; infant immunoprophylaxis remains essential; treatment usually starts ~28–32 weeks and stops at/after delivery depending on maternal indication, with monitoring for postpartum flare, renal/bone effects, and resistance. So the evidence does **not** back calling the claim false; it supports a narrower version.
